title: "Unicode, UTF-8, and text normalization"
subtitle: "An optional technical deep dive into string representation"
lang: en

This page is a **technical companion** to the [overview of the text-to-token path](text-data.qmd). It is not required to understand the general pipeline; it becomes useful when text looks identical on screen but produces different encodings or tokenization.

## Three distinct layers

- **Unicode** defines code points and properties for representing text. A code point can be written, for example, as `U+00E9`.
- **UTF-8** is an encoding that represents code points as bytes. A code point may require multiple bytes.
- **Unicode normalization** transforms some sequences into a canonical or compatibility form. It can bring equivalent strings into a common form, but must not be assumed: the policy depends on the preprocessing and tokenizer.

Unicode does not define token segmentation; UTF-8 does not choose the vocabulary; normalization is not universally applied in the same way.

## Example: two encodings of “é”

![Two visually similar forms of “é” with different code points and UTF-8 bytes.](../images/unicode-utf8-tokenization-en.svg){fig-alt="Comparison of precomposed é (U+00E9, bytes C3 A9) and e followed by a combining accent (U+0065 U+0301, bytes 65 CC 81). Normalization may bring them together before tokenization." width=100%}

The precomposed form contains one code point (`U+00E9`). The decomposed form contains `e` (`U+0065`) followed by a combining accent (`U+0301`). The visual rendering may be identical, but the code-point and byte sequences differ.

```python
import unicodedata

composed = "é"
decomposed = "e\u0301"

print([f"U+{ord(char):04X}" for char in composed])
# ['U+00E9']
print(composed.encode("utf-8"))
# b'\xc3\xa9'

print([f"U+{ord(char):04X}" for char in decomposed])
# ['U+0065', 'U+0301']
print(decomposed.encode("utf-8"))
# b'e\xcc\x81'

print(unicodedata.normalize("NFC", composed) == unicodedata.normalize("NFC", decomposed))
# True
```

NFC normalization makes these two strings equal in this example. This does not prove that a particular tokenizer applies NFC: check its documentation and test the exact version in use.

## What this implies—and what it does not

1. Visually identical strings can have different representations before normalization.
2. UTF-8 bytes are neither tokens nor vocabulary IDs.
3. A tokenizer may normalize and pre-split text before applying segmentation rules; the exact steps depend on the implementation.
4. The figure illustrates Unicode and UTF-8, **not** the output of a particular tokenizer. To inspect real tokens and IDs, run the exact tokenizer with its version and configuration.

## Technical references

- [UTF-8, RFC 3629](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3629) — specification of UTF-8 encoding.
- [Unicode Standard Annex #15](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr15/) — Unicode normalization forms.
- [Official Unicode normalization charts](https://www.unicode.org/charts/normalization/) — visual examples of normalized forms.
